<STRUCT_0001>
One motivation for the introduction of the language of schemes
is that it gives a very precise notion of what it means to
define a variety over a particular field. For example a variety
<MATH_0001> over <MATH_0002> is synonymous
(Varieties, Definition <REF_0001>)
with <MATH_0003> which is of finite type,
separated, irreducible and reduced<FOOTNOTEOPEN_0001>Of course algebraic
geometers still quibble over whether one should require <MATH_0004> to be
geometrically irreducible over <MATH_0005>.<FOOTNOTECLOSE_0001>. In any case, the idea
is more generally to work with schemes over a given <TEXTITOPEN_0001>base scheme<TEXTITCLOSE_0001>,
often denoted <MATH_0006>. We use the language: ``let <MATH_0007> be a scheme over <MATH_0008>''
to mean simply that <MATH_0009> comes equipped with a morphism <MATH_0010>.
In diagrams we will try to picture the <TEXTITOPEN_0002>structure morphism<TEXTITCLOSE_0002>
<MATH_0011> as a downward arrow from <MATH_0012> to <MATH_0013>.
We are often more interested in the properties of <MATH_0014> relative
to <MATH_0015> rather than the internal geometry of <MATH_0016>.
For example, we would like to know things about the fibres of <MATH_0017>,
what happens to <MATH_0018> after base change, and so on.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
We introduce some of the language that is customarily used.
Of course this language is just a special case of thinking
about the category of objects over a given object in a category,
see Categories, Example <REF_0002>.
